articles.title_orig: Amazon earnings live: Q3 earnings miss sends stock lower
articles.title_zh: Amazon earnings live: Q3 earnings miss sends stock lower
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Amazon ( AMZN ) reported third quarter results Thursday, missing on the top and bottom lines, sending the stock falling.
Amazon says Q4 net sales will come in between $240 billion and $247 billion versus expectations of $244.5 billion
For the quarter, Amazon saw earnings per share (EPS) of $1.89 on revenue of $201.9 billion. Analysts projected EPS of $1.97 on revenue of $202.25 billion, according to Bloomberg's analyst consensus estimates. The company reported EPS of $1.95 and revenue of $180.16 billion in the same period last year.
Amazon stock fell more than 9% on the news.
AWS revenue came in at $45.9 billion versus expectations of $45.68 billion, while online store sales hit $68.47 billion. Wall Street was anticipating $69.6 billion. Amazon's advertising business saw sales of $19.6 billion.
While Amazon's net sales increased 12%, the company noted that it would have been higher if Prime Day had taken place in Q3, like it did last year, rather than Q2.
"As a reminder, Prime Day timing shifted this year, with the event occurring in Q2 for most large countries. In 2025, Prime Day occurred entirely in Q3. Excluding this shift, third quarter year-over-year growth would have been approximately 400 basis points higher," the company said in its earnings report.
CEO Andy Jassy says Fortune 500 companies spent nearly 7x more year over year on its Bedrock inferencing service and that total Bedrock token volume grew nearly 17x.
In a quick reaction note to investors, Yorkville Ives senior managing director Dan Ives said the question for Amazon going forward is how long it can keep up AWS growth.
"AWS exited the quarter at a $184 billion annualized revenue run rate, and Jassy projected AWS revenue growth above 40% in both 2027 and 2028.
For Amazon the debate is how long AWS can run as capacity and Trainium come online, and a 39% print with management projecting more than 40% growth in both 2027 and 2028 is a stronger answer than the quarter alone."
In addition to misses on the top and bottom line for the third quarter, Amazon's outlook for Q4 sales came in between $240 billion and $247 billion, with the midpoint at $243.5 billion.
Analysts were looking for a midpoint of $244.5 billion
Amazon says it anticipates Q4 operating income of between $28.5 billion and $33.5 billion, with the midpoint falling at $31 billion. That's lower than the $32.99 billion analysts were looking for.
That's at least part of the reason for the sharp sell-off following the earnings announcement.
Amazon's all-important AWS segment continued its strong growth in Q3, with year-over-year sales of 39% to $46.0 billion.
Wall Street analysts were anticipating revenue of $45.68 billion.
In a statement following Amazon's earnings, CEO Andy Jassy said that one of the company's newer business segments could generate $1 trillion in revenue over the next decade.
Those include Amazon's grocery and pharmacy segments, its Leo satellite service, and its Zoox self-driving car business.
"Our AWS investment in functionality and infrastructure is working, with over 39% year-over-year revenue growth in Q3 ($184 billion revenue run rate) and projected revenue growth rates of over 40% both in 2027 and in 2028," Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said in a statement.
"Our broader selection and speedier delivery are helping us capture more retail market segment share with improving margins, and our newer businesses, ranging from Grocery to Pharmacy to Amazon Leo to Zoox, are progressing encouragingly. There has never been a trillion-dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years."
Bank of America expects AWS, Amazon's cloud unit, to drive upside in third-quarter results from new capacity, price increases, AI lab contracts, and growing enterprise demand.
"Ultimately, we continue to believe the biggest drivers of the stock are expectations around the AI opportunity and returns on capex," the company wrote in a note to clients. "The key risk is high expectations (possibly at 42%+), but results should suggest strong ROI on capacity capex."
Risks include rising capital spending, 4Q cost pressure from higher gas prices, and soft Q3 ad revenue, which could fuel concerns about AI shopping agents.
The company maintains its Buy rating on Amazon with a $320 target ahead of earnings.
UBS analyst Stephen Ju writes in an investor note that he'll be focusing on AWS's operating margins, which he pegs at 46% for 2027 versus street estimates of 39% as revenue continues to ramp.
Oppenheimer's Jason Helfstein concurred in a note, saying that chip efficiency and revenue growth should lead to better-than-anticipated margins going forward.
"We continue to believe AWS is well positioned to capitalize on AI demand, from workforces modernizing tasks and emerging consumer applications (e.g., AI assistants)," KeyBanc Capital Markets' Justin Patterson wrote in a note to investors.
"As agentic workloads are more CPU-intensive, AWS's Graviton chip offers both price and performance advantages and is attracting customers like Meta. Further, we believe services like Bedrock make it easy for enterprises to switch between models, providing AWS the ability to benefit from open-weight and closed-weight models," he added.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO reportedly targeted by an alleged Chinese spy
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO reportedly targeted by an alleged Chinese spy
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China
US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.
Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China , prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.
after newsletter promotion
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in a statement. Megaspeed and customers like it “receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security”.

articles.title_orig: Robust consumer spending, AI-related investment power US economy in third quarter
articles.title_zh: Robust consumer spending, AI-related investment power US economy in third quarter
articles.content_orig:

Driven by strong consumer spending and a surge in artificial intelligence investments, the U.S. economy expanded at a healthy 3.4% annualized pace between July and September, accelerating from the second quarter.
Figures released Thursday by the Commerce Department show that third-quarter gross domestic product—measuring total output across goods and services—outpaced the 2.2% growth recorded from April through June. Household spending increased at a swift 3.8% rate while business investment climbed sharply amid the boom in AI technology.
The performance demonstrates the ongoing resilience of the world’s largest economy, despite higher energy costs brought on by fighting with Iran. Growth surpassed expectations, topping the 3% expansion projected by forecasters in a survey by data firm FactSet.
Commercial investment, excluding housing, rose 12.7% as growth was lifted by AI spending. Capital outlays on information processing equipment jumped 37.4%, software rose 9.6%, and research and development increased 7.5%. Conversely, residential investment, constrained by high mortgage rates, fell 3.3%, marking its sixth decline in the last seven quarters.
Thursday’s report represents the first of three Commerce Department estimates regarding third-quarter GDP growth.
Inflation data was also released on Thursday. An inflation gauge closely monitored by the Federal Reserve accelerated last month, showing that prices remain elevated less than a week before midterm elections in which affordability concerns have become a central issue.
Consumer prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, the Commerce Department said Thursday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.5%, up from 0.3% in August and the highest figure since May.
Annual inflation has worsened since the Iran war caused spikes in oil and gas prices. U.S. oil prices still top $100 a barrel, up from less than $70 before the war. Polls show that the rise in inflation has soured most voters on the economy and President Donald Trump's handling of rising costs. Trump campaigned in 2024 on lowering prices, including bringing the cost of gas below $2 a gallon. It currently averages about $4.25 a gallon nationwide.
Excluding the volatile energy and food categories, inflation also picked up. It increased 3.1% from a year ago in September, up from 3% in August. And from August to September, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the previous month.
The reports come a day after the Federal Reserve, the agency tasked with combatting inflation, left its key interest rate unchanged. With inflation above the Fed's 2% target and the economy charging ahead, the central bank will remain under pressure to raise rates at its next meeting in December.
Thursday's inflation data comes from the personal consumption expenditures price index, which typically echoes the better-known consumer price index published earlier this month. The Fed more closely monitors the PCE index because it puts less weight on housing prices and allows for changes in consumers' shopping habits.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to host European leaders in Canada as he seeks to deepen trade ties with the EU amid Donald Trump’s ongoing economic hostility.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa will join Carney in Montreal on Thursday for a two-day summit.
It is understood the talks will aim to deepen trade, defence and economic relationships as Canada looks to secure relationships outside of Washington.
EU officials said ahead of the talks that the proposed partnership with Canada could improve the relationship more than has ever been achieved with a non-European country.
Carney said Tuesday the summit would launch further negotiations over the next year. “It doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said.
“What matters is the difference that it will make to lives of Canadians, young Canadians in terms of opportunities to study, work and travel, our Canadian businesses in terms of new opportunities, Canadian researchers in terms of depths of opportunity, and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose.”
Carney has ruled out formally joining the EU, which would require Canada to align its laws and regulations with the bloc’s.
Canadian officials said Canada would not assume the EU’s membership-related budget obligations, although it could contribute to specific programs. Carney has said any enhanced partnership would face a vote in Canada’s Parliament.
The summit puts Carney’s vision for a new global order to the test. At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January, he warned that the U.S.-led international order was breaking down and urged middle powers to unite against economic coercion.
Trump has suggested Canada’s proposed EU arrangement could be a “hostile act” and threatened tariffs on Europe if he considered it unfriendly.
Asked Wednesday about possible retaliation, a senior Canadian government official told reporters the closer relationship was not directed against the United States but reflected longstanding shared interests.
The summit is expected to launch an “Alliance for the Future,” a framework for closer cooperation on trade, defense, critical minerals, technology and research. Von der Leyen said the alliance would help Canada and Europe respond together to a world of growing rivalries.
The proposed relationship could include regular meetings between Canadian ministers and European commissioners and expanded opportunities for students through the EU’s Erasmus+ program, which supports international study and educational exchanges.
European commissioners and Canadian Cabinet ministers will hold sector-specific meetings, beginning with a business forum Thursday before formal leaders’ talks Friday. Officials hope to develop the broader partnership for possible endorsement in 2027.
Tobias Gehrke, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said the disagreement over terminology was unlikely to derail closer cooperation.
“There is no magic shortcut to rapidly reducing Europe’s and Canada’s reliance on the U.S. economy and military — not least since Washington might retaliate,” Gehrke said. “But the political window is now wide open to take a much bigger step than was previously conceivable.”
Canada has long looked to Europe to reduce its dependence on its much larger southern neighbor. “It was the idea of not being alone with the Americans that drove it,” said Robert Bothwell, a University of Toronto historian.
Carney has deep personal ties to Europe. The former Bank of Canada governor led the Bank of England from 2013 to 2020.
He chose Paris and London for his first foreign trip as prime minister rather than Washington, a break with tradition. He said the countries reflected Canada’s founding Indigenous, French and British peoples.
Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal, said Trump’s policies are accelerating Canada’s efforts to strengthen ties beyond the United States.
“The policies and rhetoric of the Trump administration are clearly pushing both Canada and the EU to imagine a world without strong U.S. leadership and to act accordingly,” Béland said.
Ottawa is reviewing plans to buy 72 additional American-made F-35 fighter jets and considering Sweden’s Saab Gripen as an alternative. Canada has committed to an initial 16 F-35s.
Canada is the only non-European country participating in the EU’s 150-billion-euro ($167-billion) SAFE defense procurement program, allowing Canadian companies to take part in joint European military purchases.
But deeper defense cooperation faces obstacles. Sundar said France is pushing for strict “Made in Europe” rules that could limit Canadian companies’ access to future EU defense spending, while Germany favors broader participation by countries outside the bloc.
He said negotiations over the EU’s next seven-year budget could matter more to Canada than anything announced in Montreal.
The two sides already have a sweeping free trade agreement, known as CETA, that eliminated most tariffs. Most provisions have been in force since 2017, although some EU member states have yet to ratify it.
The United States accounted for 71.7% of Canada’s merchandise exports in 2025. Carney wants to double exports to other countries over the next decade.
Canada and the EU are pursuing closer cooperation on digital trade and critical minerals, including possible European Investment Bank financing. Canadian officials said Wednesday they were exploring ways to stabilize mineral prices and encourage investment.
Gehrke said Europe’s growing trade confrontation with China is driving demand for Canadian critical minerals. Canada has the resources and mining expertise Europe needs, while Europe offers industrial demand, technology and capital.
Sundar said the shifting international order presents Europe with an opportunity to become a more influential global power.
“Trump’s predatory behavior is allowing the EU to position itself as an alternative geopolitical anchor,” he said.

articles.title_orig: A Chinese businesswoman who had a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, was found to be passing intelligence to Beijing.
articles.title_zh: A Chinese businesswoman who had a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, was found to be passing intelligence to Beijing.
articles.content_orig:
By WILL POTTER, US SENIOR NEWS REPORTER
Published: 09:27 EDT, 29 October 2026 | Updated: 13:07 EDT, 29 October 2026
Nvidia boss Jensen Huang sparked intelligence fears after he formed a 'close relationship' with a female spy who the CIA believed was smuggling AI microchips to China , reports say.
The AI chief, 63, reportedly alarmed the White House and US intelligence circles when it was revealed that he had formed a relationship with Chinese business executive and suspected spy Alice Huang.
As the CEO of tech firm Megaspeed, Ms Huang, of no relation to the Nvidia boss, is believed to have acted as an intermediary funneling banned AI chips to China, according to The New York Times .
The efforts allegedly violated US policies preventing Nvidia's advanced AI chips from reaching Beijing , with the company playing a central role in America's race to control the artificial intelligence industry.
Sources told the Times that the relationship only became known when an investigation was launched into Ms Huang's alleged espionage for China, and intelligence circles discovered a US citizen was 'in contact' with her.
When top officials requested to learn the name of the US citizen, they were stunned to learn that it was Jensen Huang, one of the richest and most powerful men in the world.
It is unclear when the relationship began or when it was uncovered, however, President Trump was reportedly briefed on the intelligence findings roughly one year ago, the Times reported.
Trump, who has often spoken of the vital need to win the AI race over China, chose not to act on the information related to Huang.
Nvidia boss Jensen Huang sparked intelligence fears after he formed a 'close relationship' with female spy Alice Huang (center) who the CIA believed was smuggling AI microchips to China, reports say
Huang reportedly set off alarm bells in the White House and US intelligence circles with his 'close relationship' with the suspected Chinese spy
Huang's Nvidia has grown to a market capitalization of over $5 trillion, and the company represents the central pillar in America's AI expansionist efforts.
With Trump embracing Silicon Valley and technology executives in his second term, Huang has found his way into the president's inner circle at times, often invited to the White House with other business titans.
Huang has successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen regulations on AI technology and restrictions on the sales of Nvidia chips around the world. In June, Huang revealed to The Associated Press that Trump often called him late at night to discuss AI, jobs, manufacturing and national security.
It was also revealed earlier this month that Trump bought as much as $1.6 million in Nvidia stock and sold over $1 million of the stock in August, and Trump has often placed Huang next to himself at state dinners in his second term.
But according to The New York Times, Huang's proximity to the president escalated at the same time that his 'close relationship' with Ms Huang was attracting the attention of US intelligence.
A probe into the Megaspeed CEO's ties to Beijing determined that she was gathering intelligence for China and diverting Nvidia chips into the country.
Huang has become a key business titan in Trump's second term, and the president often places himself next to the Nvidia chief at White House summits
Huang seen with his wife Lori in April 2026
Pictures posted to LinkedIn by the company NetThunder showed the Nvidia boss and Ms Huang together in a bar in Taipei in June 2024
Yet while she remains under surveillance, companies that have been affiliated with her have continued to purchase Nvidia chips this year, per the Times.
Sources told the Times that while some top American business leaders receive defense briefings if they are targeted by foreign intelligence services, Mr Huang has not received these briefings from the US.
When Trump was briefed over the claims last year, officials said they did not believe the Nvidia boss knew that Ms Huang was gathering information for Beijing.
Although it is unclear when the relationship is believed to have begun, in June 2024 the pair were seen together at a bar in Taipei following a local technology trade show.
Huang, in a black leather jacket, was seen sipping whiskey with other executives in the dark bar, as Ms Huang sat next to him. The pictures were shared to LinkedIn at the time by the company NetThunder.
A year later in May 2025, the pair were again seen leaving a restaurant together in Taipei, following a business dinner with AI suppliers. According to the Times, she waited behind for Huang as he spoke to journalists.
Nvidia said in response to the allegations that Megaspeed was like many of its regional partners, and that an internal investigation previously debunked claims it was smuggling chips into China.
Huang has made a number of appearances with Trump in his second term, and the Nvidia boss revealed earlier this year that the president often calls him late at night
Huang's Nvidia has grown to a market capitalization of over $5 trillion, and the company represents the central pillar in America's AI expansionist efforts
A spokesman for Nvidia said: 'Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.'
The spokesman added that Nvidia is 'confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.'
Megaspeed also said in a statement that its 'current leadership' was taking the matter 'extremely seriously and is committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations.'
The company added that 'outside counsel has been retained to conduct a thorough internal investigation and has notified the U.S. government that we are fully committed to cooperating.'
The Daily Mail has contacted Nvidia and the White House for comment.

articles.title_orig: Rivian third-quarter earnings beat estimates as software revenue, R2 deliveries rise
articles.title_zh: Rivian third-quarter earnings beat estimates as software revenue, R2 deliveries rise
articles.content_orig:
Rivian Automotive beat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations as it ramped up production of its new R2 entry-level SUV that the company has promised investors will lead the company to profitability.
Here's how Rivian performed in the period ended Sept. 30, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:
Shares of Rivian were up roughly 5% during afterhours trading Thursday, after hitting a new 52-week low of $11.38 earlier in the day. The stock closed at $11.45 a share, down 1.9%
The electric vehicle maker also revised its 2026 guidance to mark expected improvements in its vehicle deliveries, pre-tax adjusted earnings and capital expenditures.
The new guidance calls for a pre-tax adjusted loss of between $1.75 billion and $1.85 billion — a $100 million improvement at the midpoint from its prior guidance — vehicle deliveries of between 67,000 and 70,000 units, up from at least 65,000; and capital expenditures of between $1.4 billion and $1.5 billion, $300 million less at the midpoint.
Rivian attributed the improvement in its pre-tax adjusted earnings guidance to better-than-expected revenue related to its sales of regulatory credits, an IEEPA tariff refund receivable in the third quarter and its expected increase in vehicle deliveries.
The R2 — the first deliveries of which arrived to customers in June — has become Rivian's best-selling model and was responsible for "much of the gain quarter-over-quarter," the company said.
Rivian delivered a record 19,248 units from July through September.
The EV maker remains unprofitable overall but continued to narrow its losses during the quarter. The company reported a net loss attributable to common stockholders of $913 million, compared with a loss of $1.17 billion during the third quarter of 2025.
Rivian's gross profit, which is closely monitored by investors, was $176 million during the third quarter, up from $24 million a year earlier. Its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was a loss of $435 million, a $167 million improvement from the same period last year.
The company reported that its software and services segment continues to grow, generating $605 million in revenue and a gross profit of $256 million, a 42% margin. That compares to its automotive operations, which recorded nearly $1.55 billion in revenue and a gross loss of $80 million.
Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe has said the company will reach profitability this year on a per-unit production basis with the R2, a smaller and less expensive sibling to its current luxury R1S SUV. But he said the company needs to scale beyond current R2 production plans of 160,000 units in order to achieve profitability.
Scaringe said Thursday that the R2 will continue to assist with the company's gross profit.
"That ramp-up is critical for us getting to positive gross margin on R2 and that ultimately will contribute to positive gross margin for the business," he told CNBC's Phil LeBeau during an interview.
Rivian on Thursday reconfirmed its cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments balance was $5.5 billion, up from $5.3 billion to end the second quarter.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's Jensen Huang seen as target in China spy plot, report says
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's Jensen Huang seen as target in China spy plot, report says
articles.content_orig:
An Nvidia spokesperson on Thursday pushed back on a New York Times report that detailed American intelligence agencies surveilling a person close to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang because they thought she could be a Chinese intelligence asset.
According to the Times report , which cited people briefed on intelligence surveillance, Alice Huang, who is linked to the Singapore-based cloud Megaspeed, developed a close relationship with Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
Intelligence agencies worried that she was a spy, helping the Chinese government gain information from Nvidia and Jensen Huang, and fretted that Nvidia's CEO had access to President Donald Trump.
The Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the story in a statement to CNBC, saying that Singapore-based Megaspeed is another one of the company's regional cloud customers, and that Jensen Huang's interactions with its officials are not unusual, because he speaks with thousands of customers every year.
The spokesperson added that customers don't get access to Nvidia trade secrets or relevant national security information.
The report also alleged that Megaspeed was previously suspected of helping companies evade U.S. export controls on Nvidia's AI chips, which aren't allowed to be shipped to China.
Nvidia said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls.
"The diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year," the spokesperson said in a statement.
Nvidia implied that the U.S. government had not briefed Nvidia on Alice Huang.
"We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," the spokesperson said.
Nvidia has had to walk a tightrope in Washington as its AI chips have become a powerful tool for all AI developers and a bargaining chip in economic competition with China.
Politicians and analysts say that Nvidia's AI chips could be used to create Chinese military AI models, or commercial AI models that could compete and eventually surpass American technology.
As AI has become more important to the government, Nvidia's Huang has befriended Trump and has given pro-American speeches about building U.S. AI infrastructure.
Huang has appeared with Trump at state dinners, AI summits, and international trips, all while pushing for certain Nvidia chips to get a green light to be shipped to China.
Earlier this year the U.S. government cleared Nvidia's H200 chip to be shipped to China, but Chinese regulators prevented their imports. H200s are Nvidia's Hopper generation chip, not the current faster Blackwell generation currently used by American AI developers.
The Nvidia spokesperson said the Chinese government is not looking for Nvidia products from regional clouds like Megaspeed.
"Instead, the PRC government blocked U.S. AI chips, protecting its own industry and resulting in the largest write-offs in U.S. tech history," the Nvidia spokesperson said. Last year, Nvidia wrote off about $4.5 billion in Chinese-tuned AI chips.

articles.title_orig: Starbucks international business disappoints but U.S. stores outperform
articles.title_zh: Starbucks international business disappoints but U.S. stores outperform
articles.content_orig:
Starbucks on Thursday reported mixed quarterly results as its international cafes underperformed expectations.
However, its U.S. turnaround continues to take hold, as its home market topped expectations during the coffee giant's final quarter of fiscal 2026.
"We enter fiscal 2027 with momentum, a clear set of priorities and higher ambitions for what Starbucks can become," CEO Brian Niccol said in a video shared on the company's website.
For fiscal 2027, Starbucks is projecting adjusted earnings per share in a range of $3.15 to $3.25, above Wall Street's expectations of earnings per share of $3.14. However, its anticipated revenue decline of 1% is weaker than expected; analysts were forecasting net sales growth of 1.4%. The outlook includes an additional week and the effects of the shift in its China business to a joint venture business model.
Shares of Starbucks fell slightly in extended trading.
Here's what the company reported for the quarter ended Sept. 27 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Starbucks reported fiscal fourth-quarter net income attributable to the company of $677.2 million, or 59 cents per share, up from $133.1 million, or 12 cents per share, a year earlier.
Excluding restructuring and impairment costs and other items, the company reported earnings per share of 80 cents.
Net revenue fell 4% to $9.14 billion, reflecting the joint venture deal in China.
The company's global same-store sales increased 7.2%, fueled by growth in average ticket, and beating Wall Street estimates of 6%, according to StreetAccount. Transactions grew 1.8% in the quarter.
Starbucks' U.S. cafes reported same-store sales growth of 7.7%, topping StreetAccount estimates of a 6.5% increase.
Outside of North America, the company's international comparable sales ticked up 0.9%, as traffic declines offset an increase to average ticket. That growth fell short of analyst estimates of a 3.2% increase, according to StreetAccount.
Starbucks opened 303 net new cafes during the quarter. In September, the company announced it would close about 1% of its North American footprint, or about 250 locations, as part of its turnaround.

articles.title_orig: Polymarket trading halted after vendor compromise; impacted users will be ‘made whole’
articles.title_zh: Polymarket trading halted after vendor compromise; impacted users will be ‘made whole’
articles.content_orig:
Prediction markets platform Polymarket was forced to halt trading on its international platform Thursday for nearly an hour because of what it said was a compromise of third-party software.
There were also unconfirmed reports from users on Polymarket’s Discord channel who said their wallets had been drained.
While Polymarket did not confirm that users had lost money, it said in an X post that “anyone who has been impacted will be made whole.”
“We’ll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders,” the company said in a subsequent post on X .
Polymarket said the attack appeared to emanate from the United Kingdom and that it had referred the matter to British law enforcement authorities.
The hackers gained access to the funds via software from DebugBear, a web analytics and website performance tool, according to a person familiar with the details who was granted anonymity to address an evolving security situation.
DebugBear said on X that it was experiencing an “ongoing security incident” at around 2 p.m. ET Thursday.
Crypto news website The Block reported that some $2.65 million in cryptocurrencies had been siphoned from Polymarket users’ wallets, citing data from blockchain analysis group Arkham.
A Polymarket representative declined to comment on that figure or on the precise nature of the attack.
Polymarket said in its X post that it had identified and fixed an issue affecting its international platform, Polymarket.com.
“One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement,” Polymarket said.
“Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading & are working to bring the platform back online,” it added.
Trading began again at 3 p.m. ET after nearly an hour offline.
Polymarket’s U.S.-based platform did not appear to be affected by the breach.
Compromising third-party vendors has become a common way malicious actors gain access to large platforms and websites.
These hackers’ success in stealing money from Polymarket users, however, makes this a significant breach.
Polymarket was valued at $21 billion in September after a group of investors led by Donald Trump Jr. invested $1 billion in the platform.
The company currently processes approximately $200 million worth of trading activity daily.
Polymarket, along with rival Kalshi, has become the subject of an intense, multimillion-dollar battle between U.S. states and the Trump administration over who gets to regulate the prediction-market betting that occurs on the sites.
The platforms also continue to fight off potential insider trading activity. Earlier Thursday, Bloomberg News reported Polymarket was investigating reports of suspicious bets made amid Israel’s closely watched elections.
It is also investigating “dozens” of bets related to the U.S. midterms, according to the company’s head of global intelligence and investigations, Shana Bautista.
Earlier this month, Kalshi said it was looking into suspicious bets involving Trump’s choice for press secretary.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: Protests erupt in Spain after train crash kills dozens
articles.title_zh: Protests erupt in Spain after train crash kills dozens
articles.content_orig:
URDA, Spain — Spain began three days of mourning Thursday after at least 69 people were killed and dozens more were injured in the country’s deadliest train crash in decades . But anger is mounting about the alleged incompetence that allowed the accident to happen and protesters clashed with police overnight outside the country’s Transportation Ministry in Madrid.
Once considered one of the country’s crowning achievements, Spain’s high-speed rail network had not endured a deadly crash since it came into service over 30 years ago.
After the second train accident in less than a year , the tragedy has deepened the feeling among many that there is something broken in the Spanish transportation system.
The crash follows weeks of protests in connection to rising costs and a housing shortage, which have already triggered massive and sometimes deadly demonstrations across the country, and piled the pressure on Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
On Wednesday, four weeks before the country goes to the polls in a national election, Sanchez visited the site in the central province of Toledo, where a quiet stretch of rail lined by olive groves had been turned into a scene of devastation.
Pictures showed several carriages lying on their sides next to the tracks and others twisted at angles, their wheels sheared off. Debris was strewn around the scene of the accident, which happened after one train crashed into another that was stationary on the line.
More than 800 military and police personnel, ‌over 200 vehicles, three helicopters, a mobile command post, drones, mounted units ⁠and search dogs, were brought in to rescue survivors and recover bodies, Spain’s Interior Ministry said Thursday.
Regional leader Emiliano Garcia-Page said the death toll had risen to 69, and that human remains had been found during rescue efforts, which now involved crane operations, particularly on a carriage that remained overturned.
A judge in Toledo barred anyone not involved in emergency, security, healthcare or judicial work from the crash site ⁠with an exclusion zone of around a mile of the site.
Spain’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that 42 foreign citizens ​from seven ⁠countries were involved in the crash, of whom one was killed and at least seven injured. Authorities said 57 of those injured remained in the hospital.
Several Americans were hurt, according to the State Department, which did not provide further details.
Jacksonville, Florida, firefighter Josue Garcia-Otero was on board with seven of his family members.
“We got to safety first, then began treating other patients that were critically injured,” Garcia-Otero said in a news release issued by the Jacksonville Fire and Rescue Department. “My wife is a nurse, and she was helping too.”
Pledging an investigation and improvements to prevent a similar tragedy in future, Sánchez said “it was clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail.”
Tangui Binier, who lives in Madrid, told NBC News that he was traveling with his father when their train stopped and was struck.
“We just felt this heavy like impact from the back,” Binier, 22, said. “Everything flew forward,” he added.
Passengers did not know what to do and some were afraid because of visible live wires from the destroyed train cars, he said. Binier’s father managed to open an emergency door.
“When we got out of the train, we just looked backwards and just saw the complete mess and destruction that was behind us,” he said.
Still in shock, he and his father then quickly moved to help people get off the train, he said.
“A lot of people laying on the ground, kind of disfigured. A lot of things that are, that are really, really hard to share and... describe,” Binier said.
“I really don’t think it’s something you can prepare for,” he added.
The prime minister said it was “not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year.” In January, 46 people died in the south of the country after one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of a train going the opposite way.
Both crashes involved trains operated by the state-owned Renfe company and the privately owned IRYO.
Spain’s transportation minister, Oscar Puente, said that the crash was caused by what he called the “inexplicable” order from a central command center to resume operations after a security system had failed.
Puente, who is facing calls to resign, said the train engineers were not to blame. A security system had stopped working because of a computer malfunction, causing all trains on the line to stop at about 8:30 a.m. local time (5:30 a.m. ET).
Shortly afterward, he said, central command had told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, adding that never should have happened and it ended up colliding with the stationary IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Riot police used tear gas outside the Transportation Ministry late Wednesday after far-right protesters gathered outside and pushed against a cordon set up by officers. Some threw flares and other objects as some chanted slogans against Puente and Sánchez.
Quite what effect the accident will have on Sánchez’s political ambitions remains unclear. The prime minister called a snap election next month after his Socialist party suffered several defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country’s housing crisis.
Sanchez’s minority government had put forward two decree laws aimed at protecting tenants in the rental market after nationwide protests erupted following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her Madrid apartment . Maricarmen Abascal, who was in a wheelchair, was eventually allowed to return but died in the hospital before she could do so.
Sánchez, who took office in 2018, has weathered several crises during his premiership, including the Covid pandemic and the global inflation rise.
But he has faced attacks from right-wing parties over his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both deny. Polls show he is facing and uphill battle to win votes ahead of the election next month.
Raf Sanchez is a foreign correspondent for NBC News.
Michael Fiorentino is a London-based producer for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Some Polymarket user funds stolen by hackers, exchange referring matter to U.K. authorities
articles.title_zh: Some Polymarket user funds stolen by hackers, exchange referring matter to U.K. authorities
articles.content_orig:
Some users of prediction market platform Polymarket's international exchange had funds stolen from their accounts due to a hack an unnamed third-party provider.
Polymarket has contacted law enforcement and pledged to reimburse any trader impacted. It's unclear how many users were impacted. The company's U.S. platform was not compromised.
Traders first reported on social media platforms that they were seeing unauthorized withdrawals from their accounts on Thursday afternoon. In response, the company halted trading on its international platform.
Polymarket said that it has fixed the issue on its end, and that trading resumed at 3:00 p.m. ET.
A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that the issue stemmed from a hack of DebugBear, a website performance monitoring platform. DebugBear in a post on X said that it was impacted by a security incident on Thursday. The person familiar with the Polymarket outage said that the company referred the matter to U.K. law enforcement, as that is where DebugBear is based.
DebugBear didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
An analysis of publicly-available data by two analytics firms — Betting Intelligence and Polysights — provided to CNBC said that an account on Polymarket Thursday withdrew at least $2.7 million across 710 other wallets.
Polymarket's international prediction market exchange operates as a decentralized finance platform on the polygon blockchain and is not regulated in the U.S.
The disruption comes just days before both the company's international and U.S. exchanges are expected to see heightened volumes during the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Back in June, a similar incident happened, when Polymarket said a third party vendor had been "compromised" and that the company would refund affected users.

articles.title_orig: Why Microsoft stock isn't getting crushed like Google stock after its earnings report
articles.title_zh: Why Microsoft stock isn't getting crushed like Google stock after its earnings report
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
While Alphabet's ( GOOGL ) stock is getting crushed on Thursday after earnings, Microsoft ( MSFT ) is largely getting a pass. Another way of saying it: Microsoft shares aren't significantly trading down in sympathy. And there is one simple reason why this is the case.
Microsoft's quarter is being seen as one of higher-than-expected growth that is sustainable, while Alphabet's quarter was sluggish and hinted at slowing growth rates in coming quarters.
Microsoft's Azure sales growth came in about 300 basis points above analyst estimates. Overall sales for the important cloud business grew 48%, excluding currency fluctuations. Execs guided to 49% to 50% Azure sales growth in the current quarter, ahead of consensus estimates by four percentage points.
The company's capex came in about $5 billion below estimates, and other parts of the business showed sales upside. Sales and earnings for the quarter came in ahead of analyst forecasts.
"Net/net, these results increase our confidence in the company's ability to sustain mid/upper-teens revenue growth and that strong cost of goods sold/expense operational efficiencies should be supportive of expanding operating margins," said stifel analyst Brad Reback.
Alphabet shares tanked 12% after a third quarter that could best be characterized as a letdown, both on its own and versus Microsoft.
First, Google's search business notched sales of $63.4 billion, below the $64.9 billion expected. The miss fueled fears Google's search empire is being chipped away by the likes of Claude and ChatGPT, despite massive investment by Google.
Second, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion versus a Wall Street estimate of negative $3.5 billion. In a market getting jittery about negative free cash flow at Big Tech (see the reaction to Meta's ( META ) results last week, when it also had negative free cash flow for the first time in years), Google's print stunk up the joint.
"Alphabet's 3Q results reinforced concerns we had heading into the print, re: Search is decelerating and margins have peaked near-term. This could create an air pocket over the next 1-2 quarters as investors await signs for whether this is transitory or structural," KeyBanc analyst Justin Patterson said.

articles.title_orig: Cruise company had troubled history before abandoning passengers in Cambodia
articles.title_zh: Cruise company had troubled history before abandoning passengers in Cambodia
articles.content_orig:
A dream cruise around the world has come to an abrupt halt after two years at sea, reportedly leaving passengers scrambling to find somewhere to stay in Cambodia.
The Villa Vie Odyssey, a residential cruise ship that promised passengers the chance to make the ocean their permanent home, suspended its voyage Tuesday after its operator said soaring fuel costs had made it too expensive to continue.
CRUISE VACATION COMES TO CRASHING HALT AS SHIP SLAMS INTO 2 CARGO VESSELS
The ship was carrying 203 passengers, most of them Americans, and 156 crew members when it arrived in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, according to The Associated Press.
Passengers said they were given just seven hours' notice to leave the vessel Tuesday and had to make their own arrangements, despite the company's claims that it was helping residents find temporary accommodations.
In a statement, Villa Vie Residences, which is headquartered in Florida, announced that it had been "unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses."
The company said monthly fuel expenses per cabin had climbed from roughly $1,800 to as much as $8,000 in parts of Asia.
ANGRY CRUISE PASSENGERS SAY FRUSTRATING ISSUE SHOULD HAVE BEEN DISCLOSED BEFORE BOOKING
"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," the company said, according to the AP. "Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees."
The company added, "The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements. "
The ship first set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024, on what was supposed to be a 3 1/2-year journey around the world.
For some passengers, the ship was supposed to be their permanent home long after the initial voyage ended.
MAJOR CRUISE LINE HIKES ITS POPULAR PACKAGE PRICES IN MOVE THAT COULD HIT VACATION BUDGETS
Fox Business reported in May 2024 that Villa Vie Residences was offering lifetime access to its Odyssey cruise ship through its "Endless Horizons" program for a one-time payment of $299,999 for a single-occupancy cabin or $499,999 for double occupancy.
At the time, the experience was billed as a budget-conscious alternative to traditional retirement.
The company marketed the program to retirees concerned about inflation, rising living expenses and the possibility of outliving their savings.
CEO Mikael Petterson similarly promoted the experience as a way for retirees to live on a fixed budget without worrying about ongoing expenses.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
"For less than the price of an average home, you can secure a lifetime of experiences," Petterson said at the time.
Speaking to AP, passengers expressed disappointment over the abrupt end to their voyage .
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming who boarded the ship 17 months ago, said they purchased a cabin with plans to spend years traveling the world — but were repeatedly asked to contribute more money for fuel.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," Lynn Montoya said.
"We had hopes, but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole," the AP reported.
California sisters Carol Larson, 69, and Crystal Lavering, 72, also said they were heartbroken after spending 18 months aboard the ship.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Larson, who paid $120,000 for her cabin, said she hoped residents could buy the ship and keep the cruise going.
Despite the setback, she told the AP she had no regrets about her investment.
"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk," said Larson.
"From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth. … I still feel that way."

articles.title_orig: 'Operation Supercharge': Japan and U.S. agree to develop Japanese missile facility
articles.title_zh: 'Operation Supercharge': Japan and U.S. agree to develop Japanese missile facility
articles.content_orig:
From left, Philippines Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, Australia Defense Minister Richard Marles, Japan Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and U.S.Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth prepare to leave after posing for pictures before holding a Quadrilateral Meeting on the sidelines of the 20th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defence Ministers' Meeting (ADMM) and 13th ADMM-Plus Meetings in Cebu, Philippines, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Rolex Dela Pena/Pool EPA via AP hide caption
CEBU, Philippines — The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a Japanese facility for the joint production of advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, the Japanese defense chief said.
It is the latest move by the allies, which have repeatedly expressed alarm over China's growing assertiveness in Asia.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi made the announcement in a news conference Wednesday night in the central Philippine province of Cebu, where he met U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual meeting of Southeast Asian defense chiefs and their major Asian and Western counterparts.
Koizumi raised concern Thursday about China's increasing naval activity in southwestern Japan. He said that three Chinese destroyers and a coast guard ship together crossed the Osumi Strait south of the southern main island of Kyushu and headed east to the Pacific Ocean this week. It was the first such fleet configuration his ministry has spotted, he said.
Koizumi said he cited the incident as "an example illustrating the challenging security environment in the region" in his remark at a session Thursday. His ministry will keep watching the Chinese activity with high level of interest, he said. Japan has been accelerating military buildup in southwestern Japan to deter China.
The annual meetings aim to avert a major regional conflict and strengthen defense cooperation. On the sidelines of the meetings, however, the U.S. and China and their allies have often traded criticisms.
The missiles that will be produced as part of a joint effort called "Operation Supercharge" are essential for the F-35 fighter jets, Koizumi said. The two sides agreed to build a final assembly and inspection plant for the Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, in Japan, he said. The U.S.-made F-35s are one of the world's most advanced aircraft and are also used by the Japanese military.
During his brief meeting with Hegseth in Cebu, Koizumi said he "shared a sense of crisis … regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before."
"We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means," Koizumi said.
Hegseth renewed the Trump administration's repeated assurances of commitment to help deter aggression in the region in a separate meeting on Wednesday with ASEAN defense ministers, who were led by the host, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. Like Koizumi, Hegseth did not mention China by name in expressing his security concerns in the region.
"The approach we're taking, we describe as strong, quiet and clear," Hegseth told the ASEAN defense chiefs. "Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics to let our actions speak for themselves."
His message is "clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners," Hegseth said.
Hegseth has assured the Philippines, the oldest treaty ally of Washington in Asia, that the Trump administration will build a robust deterrence against China's increasingly aggressive actions in the disputed South China Sea. Beijing claims the busy waterway, a key global trade route, virtually in its entirety.
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles said his country's forces, along with allies like the U.S., will press on with efforts to defend the rule of law despite China's increasing assertiveness, including in the South China Sea. Australia protested last year after a Chinese J-16 fighter aircraft released flares and passed within 30 meters (100 feet) of an Australian P-8 Poseidon surveillance jet over the disputed waters.
"That doesn't deter us from doing what we need to do and that's essentially asserting the rules-based order here in the end of the Pacific," Marles told The Associated Press in Cebu on Wednesday. "Freedom of navigation on the high seas is profoundly important for Australia."
The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, all ASEAN member states, along with Taiwan, also have overlapping claims in the South China Sea. Confrontations have particularly escalated between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and navy vessels in disputed shoals and outlying waters.
Washington has warned that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces, ships and aircraft come under an armed attack, including in the South China Sea.
Beijing and Tokyo have a separate dispute over tiny Japanese-controlled islands in the East China Sea, with both sides often accusing the other of infringing on their maritime territory.

articles.title_orig: 'Why not? Australia could replicate the Canadian model'
articles.title_zh: 'Why not? Australia could replicate the Canadian model'
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has branded the Coalition “nativist and protectionist” over its resistance to a proposed European Union trade agreement, but Nationals leader Matt Canavan is doubling down and claiming Labor’s $10 billion valuation relies on figures from before Brexit.
Albanese escalated the brawl over the trade pact by seizing on internal Liberal dissent, after this masthead revealed backbencher Alex Hawke warned colleagues in a closed-door meeting that backing Canavan’s tough stance would be “nutty”.
“[Hawke] questioned why it is that Matt Canavan is making determinations without any process in their party room or their shadow cabinet,” Albanese told reporters in Canberra.
“Trade is a good thing. I thought this was resolved in the 1980s under the Hawke and Keating governments and that, since then, there was support across this parliament and across the mainstream political parties.
“This is just an excuse for going down the road of protectionist and nativist politics. Nativist politics is not in Australia’s national interest. We are a trading nation.”
Albanese, who is struggling in the polls and facing increasing criticism on inflation , tried to turn the EU deal into a political test for the opposition. Labor used nearly all its set-piece speeches in question time on Wednesday to argue for the free trade agreement.
In a press conference to spruik the under-pressure government’s agenda, Albanese cited an upcoming APEC meeting between US President Donald Trump, often described as a nativist, and Chinese leader Xi Jinping and said that at that summit “Australia wants to be ... for free and fair trade unequivocally”.
The prime minister’s attack is unlikely to sway Canavan and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. Canavan frustrated his Liberal colleagues by going out early and declaring both parties were against the deal, before the shadow cabinet or leadership group had agreed. But on the substance of the deal, most Liberals agree the proposed agreement locks future governments into the Paris climate accord, shortchanges dairy and red meat producers, and embeds contentious, pro-union labour rules.
Canavan will on Thursday expose what he claims is a “fake figure” of a supposed $10 billion gain from the trade deal. The Nationals leader, who has been needling into the deal in Senate estimates, said the figure was from 2020.
“The fake figures also include the benefits of increased exports to the UK, from when the UK was previously part of the EU, but now that is no longer the case,” he said.
“The dodgy figures were also based on predictions of enormous export increases, which aren’t possible under Labor’s [deal]. It includes a staggering 528 per cent increase in beef and sheep meat exports, an 86 per cent increase in dairy exports, a 113 per cent increase in rice exports, and a 123 per cent increase in sugar exports.
“Labor has misled the public and the Senate to declare a $10 billion so-called benefit, which never modelled the actual outcomes of the worst trade deal in Australia’s history.”
Hawke, a factional opponent of Taylor, told a Liberal-only party room meeting on Tuesday that Canavan had no right to dictate the Liberal position and said voters could see the economic damage caused by the Trump administration’s stance on tariffs and trade.
“If we don’t have our own identity on key economic issues, then the Nationals will dominate us and that will be at our expense electorally,” Hawke told his colleagues, according to sources in the room.
Hawke praised Taylor for defusing the situation when Canavan, a maverick for years before becoming leader, moved unduly quickly. The backbencher added that it would be seen as “nutty” for a free-market party to outright oppose a deal with the world’s second-biggest trading bloc.

articles.title_orig: China's Communist Party seeks to tighten discipline
articles.title_zh: China's Communist Party seeks to tighten discipline
articles.content_orig:
Chinese President Xi Jinping, center left and Zhang Shengmin, Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission second from right attend a ceremony in honor of fallen national heroes at the Monument to the People's Heroes to mark Martyrs' Day at Tiananmen Square in Beijing, Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption
BANGKOK — China's top leaders on Thursday elevated the only remaining general on the commission that oversees the country's military to the Politburo, the top governing body of the Communist Party.
The leaders also adopted a resolution on strengthening self-governance, discipline and anti-corruption in the party, as they seek to extend their grip on power.
During a four-day closed-door meeting, top Communist Party leaders deliberated on and adopted resolutions that will guide the party in the coming years. The meeting comes about a year before President Xi Jinping is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party's leader.
The party elected Gen. Zhang Shengmin, who currently serves as vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, to the Politburo. Xi had earlier purged two of China's top generals, leaving Zhang as the commission's only member besides Xi himself. It also left the Politburo without any representatives from the People's Liberation Army.
Zhang also holds a position overseeing internal discipline for the military, serving as deputy secretary of the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection.
The party said in a summary of the resolution that the tasks facing it were "increasingly arduous," such as "uniting and leading the people to safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."
It said it must step up its self-governance, which involves rooting out corruption and maintaining ideological purity.
The party should, "with an eye on enhancing its long-term governance capacity, maintain its progressive nature and purity, and its close, flesh-and-blood ties with the people," according to a summary of the resolution from the official Xinhua News Agency.
Xi has championed anti-corruption since coming to power in 2012, and has sustained a crackdown on officials for more than a decade. However, analysts say the focus now also includes underperforming officials.
Party members also reviewed the earlier purges of top members and military officials, confirming the personnel changes.
The plenum meeting revealed wider-than-expected purges, according to analysis by Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at Asia Policy who studies Chinese politics. He calculated an attendance rate of 74 percent, the lowest since the times of former leader Mao Zedong, who ran political purges regularly.

articles.title_orig: After losing his majority, Netanyahu tries to delegitimize election results
articles.title_zh: After losing his majority, Netanyahu tries to delegitimize election results
articles.content_orig:
The main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority.
Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey.
Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha.
Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament.
The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48.
On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference.
Both Arab parties strongly rejected the claim, with the Arab-majority Joint List alliance saying it was baseless.
The row is being seen by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties, thereby making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to join forces with them - which is currently his bloc's only route to power.
Arab-led parties including the Joint List headed by Yousef Jabareen (C) won a record 19 seats and could play a kingmaker role [EPA]
Israeli media reported that the CEC had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims.
Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government.
But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."
Eisenkot, who was briefed on the investigation, said "it is too early to determine what happened, or if anything happened at all," and accused Netanyahu of running "an orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results".
Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is part of the Joint List, dismissed the allegation, saying: "The losing side is constructing a racist blood libel and calling on the security agencies to use force in order to overturn the election results."
Netanyahu's attacks on Arab voters and parties have been ongoing for days. He spent much of election day posting on social media that high Arab turnout is an "emergency" and a "matter of life or death" for the Israeli right. He also shared AI-generated images of Arab voters at polling stations, in an attempt to encourage right-wingers to get out and vote.
Arab Israelis, many of whom refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up about one fifth of the country.
For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout on Tuesday was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, led by Netanyahu.
The final results offer only three plausible options for a government to be formed: a national unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but speculation has swirled in recent days that an agreement could yet be reached.
A snap poll conducted by Hebrew University showed that the most popular option for voters from every party in the opposition bloc was for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am, and supported from outside by the Joint List.

articles.title_orig: Taliban’s poppy ban falters as Afghan farmers say they can't feed their children
articles.title_zh: Taliban’s poppy ban falters as Afghan farmers say they can't feed their children
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
Opium production in Afghanistan has risen fivefold in a year. According to a UN survey released on Thursday, it’s the first significant increase since the Taliban banned poppy cultivation in 2022.
The UN Office on Drugs and Crime ( UNODC ) found that the area planted with opium poppy grew by 330 per cent , to more than 43,000 hectares, up from about 10,000 hectares in 2025.
Estimated production rose by 400 per cent, from about 300 tonnes to just under 1,500 tonnes .
Both figures remain well below levels before the ban, when some 232,000 hectares were under cultivation.
For decades, Afghanistan was the world’s biggest source of illicit opium. Before the ban, it accounted for around 80 per cent of global supply.
The Taliban seized power in August 2021. In April 2022, they outlawed poppy cultivation and all narcotics, citing religious grounds.
The de facto authorities say they eradicated 22,000 hectares of poppy this year. But UNODC said many farmers appear to have adapted to evade enforcement . Some are hiding small plots within cereal fields or inside walled compounds . Others are planting and harvesting at staggered intervals to avoid detection.
“The fourfold increase in opium poppy cultivation shows the difficulty in sustaining decreases in illicit opium cultivation when poor farmers have no alternatives to feed their families ,” said UNODC Executive Director Monica Juma.
She urged the de facto authorities and the international community to work together to support farming communities, by investing in livelihoods, farm infrastructure and access to markets.
Cultivation spread to 16 of Afghanistan’s 34 provinces, five more than last year . Three in every four hectares were in the northeast, now firmly the country’s main growing area. Before the ban, most poppy was grown in the southwest.
Prices dipped from $570 a kilogramme last year to $500 but remain far above pre-ban levels of under $100 . UNODC said large regional price differences may encourage trafficking from the northeast to the southwest.
The survey said traffickers in the region appear to have relied on opium stockpiles to keep supplies moving since the ban.
But recent seizure data suggest those stocks are running down. The 2026 World Drug Report also found early signs that heroin supplies in Europe are falling.
With demand holding up and prices high, shrinking supplies could push cultivation in Afghanistan higher still.
“ International cooperation is needed to investigate and dismantle transnational drug trafficking networks both in Afghanistan and the rest of the world,” Ms. Juma said.
UNODC said continued monitoring would show whether this year’s jump is temporary or the start of a resurgence in opium and heroin production.

articles.title_orig: The average 30-year US mortgage rate dips to 7.24%, the lowest level in more than a month
articles.title_zh: The average 30-year US mortgage rate dips to 7.24%, the lowest level in more than a month
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates fell for the second straight week, and that finally brought consumers back to their brokers. A growing share, however, applied for riskier loans at even lower rates.
Total mortgage application volume rose 3.4% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, decreased to 7.37% from 7.41%, with points increasing to 0.76 from 0.75, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment.
"The decline in rates gave borrowers some relief, with applications rebounding slightly, particularly conventional applications," said Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the MBA, in a release. "Mortgage rates are still more than a percentage point higher than the same week last year and most homeowners still have rates much lower than prevailing market rates."
And that is why refinance is still running well behind where it was last year. Applications to refinance a home loan climbed 3% for the week but were 61% lower than the same week one year ago. About half of all borrowers today have a mortgage rate below 4%, according to data from the Federal Housing Finance Agency's National Mortgage Database.
Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home rose 4% for the week but were still 18% lower than the same week one year ago. While mortgage rates have pulled back some in the last few weeks, they are still much higher than they were just a few months ago, and home prices are still rising. Potential homebuyers are also worried about the broader economy, and, anecdotally, some agents say buyers are waiting to see the results of the midterm elections.
CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.
Subscribe here to get access today .
As borrowers search for savings, more are opting for adjustable-rate mortgages. The ARM share of applications increased to 11.3% last week, the highest level in more than a year. The average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs decreased to 6.41% from 6.46%. ARMs are considered riskier because they adjust to whatever the current market rate is at the end of their fixed term.
Mortgage rates haven't moved at all to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily. That is because there has not been much economic data for the bond market to react to. While the Federal Reserve is not expected to announce any change in its interest rate at Wednesday's meeting, markets could move on any commentary from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh .

articles.title_orig: Greek container ship sinks after drone attack off Bulgaria
articles.title_zh: Greek container ship sinks after drone attack off Bulgaria
articles.content_orig:
The Greek-owned, Israeli-operated vessel sank off Bulgaria after being struck by three naval drones, as suspicions grow over Russian involvement in a wave of Black Sea shipping attacks
Israeli-operated cargo ship, the Contship Jet, was struck by unidentified naval drones in the Black Sea off Varna, Bulgaria, on Wednesday.
The Contship Jet, a Greek-owned, Israeli-operated cargo ship, departed Haifa on Sunday bound for Constanta, Romania, just north of where it sank.
The Bulgarian Navy said the ship was struck by three unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) at roughly noon local time, sinking hours later and taking 421 containers with it.
All crew members were rescued unharmed, ZIM announced.
Immediately following reports of the attack, French maritime patrol aircraft conducted reconnaissance missions in the area and supported rescue efforts.
The Contship Jet is the ninth civilian ship struck this month alone in the Black Sea, leaving over 30 sailors dead.
This attack comes as the defence ministers of Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey were meeting to discuss maritime security in the Black Sea.
Suspicion has fallen on Russia over the attacks, although Bulgaria’s government has been reluctant to assign blame.

articles.title_orig: At least 14 people killed in Russian attack on Dnipro train station
articles.title_zh: At least 14 people killed in Russian attack on Dnipro train station
articles.content_orig:
Russian attacks across Ukraine have killed at least 19 people, including 14 at a busy platform in the main train station in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, officials said.
State rail company Ukrzaliznytsia said on Thursday that a jet-powered Russian drone hit the platform where a train was preparing to leave for the nearby city of Zaporizhzhia.
Regional Governor, Oleksandr Hanzha, said on Telegram that at least 14 others were injured and six were in critical condition, including an 11-year-old boy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denounced the attack as “horrific”.
“Just how many terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on certain Russian oligarchs and the Russian energy sector, rather than de-escalating?,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said Ukraine is experiencing a rise in attacks on its transport infrastructure.
“This marks a trend that we’ve seen lately here in Ukraine of Russian strikes targeting not only the country’s infrastructure, including energy installations, but also increasingly some of its transport logistics like railway stations and sometimes even those railways themselves,” MacAlpine said.
“Also, there has been a larger trend of mounting civilian casualties, according to UN human rights monitoring. Both Russia and Ukraine have seen their deadliest year of the war so far. This is all part of an upward trend that we’ve really noted here in Kyiv, with many, many attacks,” she added.
In Chernihiv in northern Ukraine, two teenagers were killed in a Russian attack on Thursday, while three people were killed in a separate strike on an apartment building in the central city of Kremenchuk.
Russia also targeted Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-biggest city, damaging an educational institution, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said on Telegram.
Russian news agencies, citing the Ministry of Defence, reported that its forces struck a cargo vessel used by the Ukrainian military in the Black Sea.
Meanwhile, Russia downed most of the 613 drones launched towards Moscow overnight, in a major attack on the Russian capital, state news agency TASS reported.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram that air defence forces destroyed 231 of the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) on approach to the city, with the remainder neutralised on distant approaches between Wednesday evening and Thursday morning.
The Kremlin condemned the attacks on Moscow as the city hosts more than 22 African leaders at a summit, TASS reported.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was “very strange” for Kyiv to target Moscow during this time.
The Russian Defence Ministry said its air defence intercepted and destroyed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight across regions.
Debris from downed drones also caused minor damage after falling onto the territory of an unnamed industrial facility in Sterlitamak, the second-largest city in Russia’s Bashkortostan region, Mayor Emil Shaimardanov said on Telegram.
He said the plant was operating as usual and that local air defence forces had shot down all eight Ukrainian drones involved in the attack.
The attack marks the latest in a series of major drone assaults targeting the Moscow region, following a record attack in September during which air defence forces reported shooting down more than 1,600 drones.
Both sides have reported an increase in attacks in recent months, while Moscow and Kyiv also prepare to resume peace talks next month with US mediation.
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian delegation has headed to the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky, where a localised ceasefire is under way to provide humanitarian aid to the remaining residents.
The Kremlin also said it hopes aid will reach Oleshky on Thursday or Friday and that those wanting to leave the town were able to do so, Russia’s Interfax news agency reported.
So far, neither Ukraine nor Russia has reported any violations of the six-day ceasefire, which took effect early Tuesday.
